elements.quote: System dynamics modeling for cancer prevention and control: A systematic review
elements.reason: The title of the article, which is included in the abstract section, explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review.

elements.quote: System dynamics modeling, which consists of diagramming and simulation approaches for understanding and managing such complexity, is being increasingly applied to cancer prevention and control, but the breadth, characteristics, and quality of these studies is not known.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies the objective of the review: to understand the breadth, characteristics, and quality of system dynamics modeling studies in cancer prevention and control.
The abstract does not specify the main inclusion and exclusion criteria (e.g., publication date range, language, study design).

elements.quote: We searched PubMed, Scopus, APA PsycInfo, and eight peer-reviewed journals to identify cancer-related studies that used system dynamics modeling.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies the information sources used, but it does not report when each source was last searched.

elements.quote: Included studies were assessed using quality criteria adapted from prior literature and mapped onto the cancer control continuum.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies that quality criteria adapted from prior literature were used to assess the included studies.

elements.quote: Characteristics of studies and models were abstracted and qualitatively synthesized.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies that the results were qualitatively synthesized.

elements.quote: 32 studies met our inclusion criteria.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (32), but it does not report the total number of participants or summarize relevant study characteristics (other than mentioning the topics and continuum areas).

elements.quote: A mix of simulation and diagramming approaches were used to address diverse topics, including chemotherapy treatments (16%), interventions to reduce tobacco or e-cigarettes use (16%), and cancer risk from environmental contamination (13%). Models spanned all focus areas of the cancer control continuum, with treatment (44%), prevention (34%), and detection (31%) being the most common.
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcomes (topics and continuum areas).
No meta-analysis was conducted.
The review did not compare groups in a way that requires reporting a direction of effect.

elements.quote: The quality assessment of studies was low, particularly for simulation approaches. ... Prior efforts have been hampered by a lack of rigor and transparency regarding model development and testing.
elements.reason: The abstract summarizes important limitations of the included evidence (low quality, lack of rigor/transparency).

elements.quote: System dynamics modeling can illustrate complex interactions and help identify potential interventions across the cancer control continuum. ... Supportive infrastructure for increasing awareness, accessibility, and further development of best practices of system dynamics for multidisciplinary cancer research is needed.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and their implications.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.

elements.quote: The study was not registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) as it was a methods review and did not assess health outcomes.

elements.quote: Cancer is a complex, multilevel phenomenon [1-5] in which health outcomes depend on highly interrelated elements across stages of etiology, prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment, survivorship, and end-of-life care [6, 7]. Standard bench and clinical research approaches alone are not well suited to account for this complexity... Systems models, particularly well calibrated simulation models, provide a relatively lowcost and low-risk opportunity for comparing potential interventions or treatments in silico... Although system dynamics modeling has been utilized in various aspects of public health since the 1970s, past reviews in this field have noted a significant increase in their use since the early 2000s, especially in areas focused on chronic or non-communicable diseases [24, 25]. The extent to which system dynamics modeling has been applied specifically to cancer prevention and control has not been studied.
elements.reason: The introduction describes the complexity of cancer, the limitations of current research approaches, the potential of systems models, and explicitly identifies the gap in knowledge regarding the application of system dynamics modeling to cancer prevention and control.

elements.quote: To overcome persistent barriers to providing high-quality, equitable care, approaches are needed to address this complexity and provide guidance for successful intervention. ... The Journal of the National Cancer Institute published several reports calling for the use of complex, multilevel, or systems-focused approaches to advance the landscape of cancer prevention and control [1, 2, 10].
elements.reason: The text explains the need for the review by highlighting the persistent barriers in cancer care and the calls from the scientific community for systems-focused approaches.

elements.quote: Although system dynamics modeling has been utilized in various aspects of public health since the 1970s, past reviews in this field have noted a significant increase in their use since the early 2000s, especially in areas focused on chronic or non-communicable diseases [24, 25]. The extent to which system dynamics modeling has been applied specifically to cancer prevention and control has not been studied.
elements.reason: The authors acknowledge existing reviews in the broader field of public health and clarify that the specific application to cancer prevention and control has not been studied, thus justifying the need for this specific review.
This is a methods review of system dynamics modeling, not a review of the effects of a specific intervention.

elements.quote: Included articles: 1) were published in peer-reviewed journals; 2) were written in English; 3) used system dynamics modeling (i.e., causal-loop diagramming, stock-and-flow diagramming, or computational system dynamics modeling); 4) pertained to cancer prevention or control; and 4) were published within the last 10 years.

elements.quote: As shown in Fig 1, most studies included a computational system dynamics simulation model (n = 21; 66%), while the remaining studies (n = 11; 34%) used only diagramming approaches (referred to as diagram-only studies in this review).

elements.quote: In their review of system dynamics models pertaining to public health and medicine, Darabi and Hosseinichimeh [17] identified a handful of studies using system dynamics modeling to replicate clinical trials and simulate different interventions related to cancer, noting that this area is 'generally underexplored' and would likely benefit from further development of models for cancer screening and treatment. Similar to the findings of our paper, this review found that only a fraction of disease-related modeling studies published their model equations and methodology for development. In a scoping review of system dynamics studies related to addiction, Naumann and colleagues [65] found similarly that the method has been underutilized and that participant engagement should be further used in future studies. In their review of system dynamics models used to assess economic efficiency in public health, Jadeja and colleagues [11] also found underutilization of participatory approaches.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly compares its findings with other relevant evidence, including reviews by Darabi and Hosseinichimeh, Naumann and colleagues, Jadeja and colleagues, Zanker and colleagues, and Stange and colleagues, to interpret the results in a broader context.
